headline: Approved authorizing signing of Preferred Schematic Report and Grade Reconfiguration Letter for proposed school at 115 Sycamore Street, 8-1 vote.
summary: The meeting covered a proposed school project at 115 Sycamore Street. The design team showed examples from other schools, and members discussed the building's size and design. Members voted 8 to 1 to authorize the Chair and Superintendent to sign the Preferred Schematic Report and Grade Reconfiguration Letter.
decisions: Approved authorizing the School Committee Chair and Superintendent to sign the Preferred Schematic Report and Grade Reconfiguration Letter for the proposed school at 115 Sycamore Street, 8 yes to 1 no.

plain_text:
1 
 
  
 
CITY OF SOMERVILLE, MASSACHUSETTS 
SCHOOL COMMITTEE 
 
     Monday, August 17, 2025 – Special Meeting of the Whole 
 
 
7:00 p.m. – Zoom Webinar  
 
I. Call to Order 
The Special Meeting of the Somerville School Committee was called to order on August 17, 2026. 
Members present: President Davis, SC Rep Pitone, SC Rep Lippens, SC Rep Eldridge, SC Rep Green, Dr. 
Stellman, Mayor Wilson, Vice Chair Biton, and Chair Ackman 
 
II. MSBA 
Chair Ackman; The meeting was convened for the purpose of considering the School Committee's vote 
regarding the Massachusetts School Building Authority (MSBA) process and the Preferred Schematic Report 
and Grade Reconfiguration Letter for the proposed school project at 115 Sycamore Street.   
 
MOTION: There was a motion by Rep Lippens, seconded by Rep Green to authorize the School Committee 
Chair and Superintendent to sign the Preferred Schematic Report and Grade Reconfiguration Letter.  
 
Prior to the vote, the Committee received a presentation from the Perkins Eastman design team addressing 
questions raised during the previous School Committee meeting regarding the proposed school's cafetorium, 
sensory spaces, breakout spaces, and classroom learning environments. 
 
The design team presented examples from other schools to illustrate potential approaches to: 
 
Cafetorium design and acoustics 
Flexible and adaptable dining spaces 
Different seating configurations for students 
Sensory-sensitive and respite spaces 
Small-group and breakout learning areas 
Student collaboration spaces 
Bringing natural daylight into interior areas 
Creating smaller, more intimate "neighborhood" spaces within a larger school 
 
The design team emphasized that the current feasibility phase is conceptual and that significant additional 
design work would be undertaken to develop spaces specifically for Somerville. 
 
Comments/ Questions 
 
Rep. Pitone thanked the design team for sharing the examples, noting that the Committee had raised 
questions about supporting sensory-sensitive students, creating an inclusive environment, and providing a 
variety of spaces to meet different student needs. 
 
President Davis expressed appreciation for the design examples but raised concerns regarding the 
proposed school's acoustics, scale, and ability to provide an inclusive environment for younger students and 
students with sensory sensitivities. He noted that while som e of the cafeteria designs appeared effective,
2 
 
  
he remained concerned about the practicality of sensory and breakout spaces within a large, highly 
structured school environment. He also questioned whether examples from other communities adequately 
reflected the conditions and scale of the proposed Somerville school and stated that the presentation did 
not sufficiently address his concerns regarding the overall size, layout, lighting, and six-story design of the 
building. 
 
Dan: the images represented schools of various sizes and were based on feedback from different 
communities. He emphasized that the design would incorporate the Committee’s input and priorities to 
create an effective learning environment for all students. 
 
Dr. Stellman: Asked for clarification on the size and grade levels of the schools shown in the examples 
to better understand their scale. She noted that parents and community members have expressed 
concerns about the intimacy and overall feel of larger schools, explaining that hearing a school has 1,000 
students can be difficult to visualize. She asked how the images could help the School Committee better 
understand what that scale looks and feels like, particularly in a K–8 setting where middle school and 
younger students may have separate spaces. She also asked whether one of the images shown was the 
new Tobin School in Cambridge and how examples from other communities could be applied to 
Somerville’s specific circumstances. 
Lisa Pecora: The examples included a PK–8 school serving more than 900 students, as well as middle and 
high school spaces featuring various seating options and acoustic features. The team noted that these 
examples could continue to serve as precedents throughout the design process, allowing the Committee 
to compare and evaluate potential solutions through drawings and photographs. They also suggested 
visiting similar schools and speaking with teachers and principals to better understand what works, what 
does not, and why. Additionally, the team offered to visit Somerville’s existing K–8 schools with the 
Committee to learn from the district’s current experiences and help inform future design decisions. 
Vice Chair Biton: Thanked the design team for sharing the images and expressed appreciation for the 
visual examples. He shared her optimism about the space being developed and stated that he looks 
forward to continued engagement throughout the process. 
Rep. Lippens: Echoed the comments regarding the design team’s work and emphasized the importance 
of creating a space that responds to the needs of the Somerville community. She noted the many 
opportunities presented by the proposed design and shared her experience visiting a PK–8 school in 
Cambridge that serves a large number of students, including students with significant challenges and 
needs. She described the space as beautiful and well-equipped to meet the needs of its students. Rep. 
Lippens encouraged fellow School Committee members and others to consider visiting the school to 
gather ideas and engage more deeply in the design process. 
Rep. Eldridge: Thanked the design team for their work and acknowledged the extensive materials 
prepared for the Committee. She referenced the National School Boards Association article Schools as 
Critical Community Infrastructure and asked the design team to speak about how school design can 
support students’ academic, social-emotional, and basic needs. 
The design team highlighted the importance of flexible breakout spaces that support different learning 
styles, encourage collaboration, and create smaller, connected communities within a larger school. They 
explained that these spaces can serve as a “front porch” for grade-level neighborhoods and provide 
students with a sense of community and belonging. The team agreed to share the article with the 
Committee.
3 
 
  
President Davis: Thanked the Chair and reiterated his concern that, while the design team has done an 
excellent job with the assignment, he believes the underlying proposal is misguided. He expressed 
concern that the nearly 1,000-seat school is too large and does not align with Somerville’s tradition of 
offering a range of school sizes and environments to meet different student needs. He questioned 
whether a school of this size, with five classes per grade in a multi-story building, could provide the 
intimate, small-school environment discussed throughout the presentation. He also raised concerns about 
the potential increase in traffic and its impact on the City’s recent progress in reducing traffic fatalities. He 
emphasized that the vote is not about specific design features, but rather whether to submit a nearly 
1,000-seat building to the MSBA as the district’s preferred approach. He urged the Committee to revise 
the submission to the smaller, approximately 600-seat option and, after rebuilding Winter Hill, turn its 
attention to addressing the long-term needs of the district’s other smaller schools. 
President Davis: concluded by stating that he believes moving forward with the current proposal would 
be a mistake and expressed his hope that the Committee would reconsider the approach. 
Rep. Pitone: Provided context on the multi-year process leading to the current proposal and noted that 
the Construction Advisory Group, School Committee, and Mayor had previously supported the larger 925-
seat school option. She identified accessibility and cost as key factors, emphasizing that fully addressing 
accessibility needs requires appropriate spaces and services beyond basic features such as elevators. She 
noted that making the Brown School fully accessible was estimated to cost approximately $94 million 
while significantly reducing outdoor space. She acknowledged concerns about the school’s size but stated 
that, given the decisions already made and the lack of a cost-effective alternative addressing the district’s 
accessibility needs, she supports moving forward with the proposal. She also noted that a larger school 
could provide greater opportunities for inclusion, particularly for students with special needs. 
Rep. Green: Thanked everyone involved and noted that concerns about the Brown School’s long-term 
sustainability have been discussed for many years. She emphasized that the district has a rare opportunity 
through the MSBA process to address several systemic issues at once. He also stated that he believes the 
Brown School’s strong academic performance should not be attributed solely to its small size and noted 
that Winter Hill is also a small school. He argued that the district must address longstanding patterns of 
segregation and create more equitable educational opportunities for all students. He highlighted the 
extensive community and professional input that has supported the current proposal, including previous 
unanimous votes by the School Building Committee and prior School Committee votes.  
Rep. Green expressed strong support for moving forward and committed to helping ensure the new 
school meets the needs of every student. 
Dr. Stellman: Asked President Davis whether he intended to make a different motion proposing the 
approximately 600-seat school option. She sought clarification on the procedural implications of his 
comments and whether he was simply expressing opposition to the current proposal or advocating for an 
alternative that would require a separate vote. 
President Davis: Clarified that the current motion would need to be tabled before a separate motion 
could be considered. He stated that he would be willing to propose revising the MSBA submission to 
recommend the approximately 600-seat option if there was interest from other Committee members. 
He reiterated that the future of the Brown School should be addressed separately from the Winter Hill 
project and clarified that he supports ultimately renovating or replacing the Brown School. He also noted 
that the School Committee previously voted on a draft based on the Construction Advisory Group’s work, 
rather than directly on a CAG recommendation, and expressed concerns about the process.
4 
 
  
President Davis concluded by stating that he would support revisiting the MSBA submission if other 
Committee members were open to considering the smaller option. 
Mayor Wilson: Thanked the Committee and members of the public for their engagement and noted the 
strong community support for the schools. He emphasized that each advisory or decision-making body 
that has considered the 690-seat versus 925-seat options has supported the larger school by a substantial 
majority, including the CAG, School Building Committee, and School Committee. 
Mayor Wilson stated that while reasonable differences of opinion remain, there is a clear and consistent 
preference for the 925-seat option at Sycamore. He expressed his support for moving forward with the 
preferred schematic report as an important step toward building the school the city needs. 
Rep. Biton: Thanked colleagues for their thoughtful comments and acknowledged the differing 
perspectives on the school size. he stated that, despite some reservations, he will support the 
Committee’s consensus to move forward with the larger school option and focus on creating the best 
possible school at the selected site. He expressed enthusiasm about the proposed design elements and 
the future of the project. 
Rep. Green: Responded to comments regarding the Committee’s previous votes and emphasized that 
those decisions were made with full consideration of the Brown School’s future and the concerns of the 
Brown community. She acknowledged that school closures can bring grief and frustration but stated that 
the Committee has consciously considered the implications of its decisions. 
Rep. Green: clarified that the 925-seat figure represents the potential capacity of the building and does 
not necessarily mean that 925 students would be enrolled there. He emphasized that a larger building 
provides greater flexibility to meet different student needs and accommodate programs, services, and 
spaces that are difficult to provide within the district’s existing facilities. He also noted that space is a 
significant limitation in Somerville and stated that the MSBA opportunity provides the district with an 
important chance to expand its capacity.  
Rep. Green concluded that the district should take advantage of the opportunity and be responsible 
stewards of its resources. 
Dr. Stellman: Reinforced the importance of addressing inequities and segregation within Somerville’s 
schools and ensuring that schools better reflect the diversity of the community. She acknowledged the 
strong emotional connection families have to their schools and recognized that changes to a school can 
bring a genuine sense of grief and loss. 
Dr. Stellman emphasized that, as a School Committee member, she has a responsibility to consider the 
needs of the entire city while also listening to constituents and families. She acknowledged the disruption 
facing Winter Hill families and expressed concern that the district has not addressed the situation more 
quickly. She concluded by emphasizing the importance of listening to voices from across the city and 
working toward a more equitable school system. 
Rep. Eldridge: Encouraged members of the community to review the National School Boards Association 
article, noting its research on trauma-informed and dignity-centered school design. She emphasized the 
importance of intentionally designing a school that meets the needs of all students and provides 
supportive spaces for everyone. Rep. Eldridge thanked the design team and Committee members for their 
work and thoughtful discussions and expressed enthusiasm about continuing the process to ensure the 
district’s schools meet the needs of all learners.
5 
 
  
 
Dr. Ackman: There being no further discussion, the Committee returned to the motion made by Rep. Lippens 
and seconded by Rep. Green: 
 
Motion: To authorize the School Committee Chair and Superintendent to sign the Preferred Schematic 
Report and Grade Reconfiguration Letter. 
 
Roll call vote: – President Council Davis- N, Member Lippens- Y, Member Eldridge-Y, Mayor 
Wilson-Y, Member Biton-Y and Dr. Ackman-Y, Dr. Stellman Member Green, Member Pitone, 
Motion passed Yes: 8 No: 1, unanimously. 
 
III. ADJOURNMENT 
 
Meeting was adjourned 7:00 p.m.
